argument: Charles Taylor's The Varieties of Religion Today takes William James's famous claim that religion is at its core a personal experience of the divine and argues that, while James brilliantly predicted how modern people would see religion, his view is too narrow because it ignores religion's sociological role. Tracing religion's evolution from paleo-Durkheim societies where living at all meant participating in religion, through neo-Durkheim societies like the United States, to a post-Durkheim world where expressive individualism makes religion an a la carte personal choice, Taylor shows what is lost when the community element disappears: accountability to something greater than one's own opinion, and the group settings that often lead to divine experience in the first place. He closes by describing the uniquely modern fragility of belief and unbelief in a structurally pluralistic world, where more and more people live on the cusp between the two, buffeted by cross-pressures that make deep commitment harder than ever.
keyIdeas: William James defined religion as a personal experience in the heart of an individual connecting to the divine, and saw institutional forms as distortions that arise when a founder's insight must be retold, written down, and turned into doctrine for everybody.

There are two valid answers to whether to live as though there is something transcendent: a closed, immanence-based stance that derives values from this world, and James's open stance that some knowledge, like trust, only becomes visible once you participate and commit.

The criticism that religion is just a security blanket against meaninglessness projects a modern bias onto history; for a medieval Dominican monk, cosmic meaning was so baked into everything that the thought of meaninglessness simply was not persuasive.

Religion's sociological function has evolved from paleo-Durkheim societies where participating in society was participating in religion, through neo-Durkheim societies where religion still unifies but is not required, to a post-Durkheim world where expressive individualism makes religion as a la carte as fashion or a toaster.

Without a community holding you accountable to something higher, whether religious or secular like a scientist's or activist's community, people settle for cheap pseudo-spiritual substitutes and endless self-excuses, while structural pluralism leaves belief and unbelief more fragile than ever, with modern people living on the cusp between them.

terms.def: The idea that there is something beyond this world which, though not directly accessible, gives meaning and order to the things in this world.
Deriving meaning and values entirely from this world as it unfolds in front of us, from things already happening that we already care about.
Taylor's name for the agnostic veto: a refusal on principle to believe in transcendent things that lack evidence, holding that this world is enough as it is.
An earlier form of society where doing almost anything meaningful, from marriage to school, assumed an embedded religion, so living in the society was itself participating in religion.
The modern condition where being part of society requires no religious participation at all, so religion becomes an entirely personal, a la carte choice made by the individual.
The modern trend, tied to the age of authenticity and consumerism, in which every choice from fashion to religion becomes a personal statement about who you are deep down.

anchors: It’s a PERSONAL EXPERIENCE, when an INDIVIDUAL feels a CONNECTION to WHATEVER it is they call the divine.
the story has to get RETOLD, which means it gets watered down, eventually it needs to get WRITTEN down, eventually turned into a doctrine. Doctrine that has to apply to EVERYBODY now.
If this person CAN’T find meaning in something TRANSCENDENT…then they will HAVE to find the meaning in their life through IMMANENCE.
there’s KINDS of knowledge… that REQUIRE the participation of the KNOWER IN something, for the knower to able to RECEIVE that knowledge.
the thought that everything is meaningless, doesn’t even FEEL to them like a philosophical POSITION that it’s worth losing SLEEP over.
a society where religion is STILL a part of what UNIFIES people in it, broadly speaking…but the actual PARTICIPATION in the RELIGION…is not REQUIRED of people as much as it was before.
why WOULDN’T religion become something to us that’s AS a la carte…as what kind of WATCH you are gonna wear or something?
Consider how a scientist for example…needs a COMMUNITY of other SCIENTISTS, all WORKING toward a similar GOAL, and all holding each other ACCOUNTABLE to an ideal of truth.
modern people can SETTLE, for a cheap kind of PSEUDO-spiritual experience, that they MISTAKE as the pinnacle of what’s POSSIBLE, because it’s just the most they’ve ever demanded of themselves.
there’s so MANY different valid ways of viewing reality that we can be EXPOSED to…that this makes belief on either SIDE of this question, something very fragile in practice.

religion is also, IMPORTANTLY something…that helps constitute, social solidarity. Meaning religion provides people a level of shared meaning, shared priorities, rites and ceremonies, religion is something that binds otherwise individual people, together into a “we”.

in SOME places, like say, in modern Europe Taylor says…we’re now in a spot where BEING part of a society… doesn’t require you to participate in ANY religious tradition… or to USE religious language at all…RELIGION’S function then for a GROWING number of PEOPLE today…becomes almost ENTIRELY a personal choice, that’s to be made by an individual.

People today’ll say things like “I’m spiritual, but not religious.” You know, a thing to say that’s an absolute HALLMARK of our ERA Charles Taylor thinks. But first of all what exactly does any of that they just said even really MEAN…and second what totally personal CHOICE did that person make that supposedly GROUNDS that kind of statement?
Declare yourself one or the other, label the other side as stupid and misguided, and then bask in your hot tub of moral superiority for the rest of your life.
James is our great philosopher of the cusp. He tells us more than anyone else about what it’s like to stand in that open space and feel the winds pulling you now here, now there.
Identity politics, nationalism, cults of personality: ALL of these different sociological functions of religion co-exist to some degree.
Pick a path that GENUINELY challenges you, whether that’s religious or secular, doesn’t matter.

the VERY FACT…that I’m the kind of creature that is SO DRAWN to this idea that there IS something transcendent, beyond this world…THAT MAY BE justification ENOUGH, for me to EXPLORE something like religion that TALKS about it so much.

what follows from here… is NOT gonna be an argument from Taylor about how you should be living your life…it’s not a prescription from him, but more a DESCRIPTION, of the MANY SIDES there are to WHAT religion IS

there’s two fairly common ways to answer it he says. BOTH of which are VALID. But while neither of these ways of thinking is WRONG, to Charles Taylor, Willam James, there WILL be a lot more to say about the details of BOTH of these and how they’re LIVED by people.
